summary: Deep dive on p95/p99 tail latency for Vectora's low-latency chat assistant. Covered streaming vs non-streaming, KV cache behavior, batching trade-offs, quantization effects, and VPC/on-prem networking hops. Agreed to run benchmarks with provided traces and schedule on-prem pilot.
topics: quantization impacts on latency and throughput
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Alright everyone, thanks for joining, we'll kick off. I'm Maya from Redwood, AE on the account, with Raj our SE and Sofia from success.
[00:08] Liam O'Connor: Hey thanks, Liam here, CTO at Vectora. We've got Evelyn SRE and Marco infra and Hannah product. Goal today is p99 tail — our customers are noticing spikes.
[00:20] Raj Patel: Great, can you give quick numbers? p95/p99 right now and in what context — streaming chat or non-streaming batch?
[00:30] Evelyn Park: Yeah currently in prod: p95 ~ 180ms, p99 ~ 430ms for our short-turn chat (avg token lengths ~ 20-60). But for longer context flows p99 jumps to 1.2s. These are streaming responses where users see tokens as they come.
[00:45] Raj Patel: OK got it. Are you doing prefix reuse / KV cache on your side or is every req cold?
[00:52] Marco Diaz: Mostly cold today; we tried prefix caching but it was inconsistent because our routing across pods evicts the KV cache, so the hit rate is low.
[01:05] Maya Chen: Right, so a few main things affect tail: KV cache hit rate, batching behavior (esp. dynamic continuous batching), quantized kernel throughput, and network hops — especially with a VPC/on-prem fronting.
[01:18] Hannah Lee: Quick Q — team asked whether streaming vs non-streaming changes p99 significantly?
[01:23] Raj Patel: Yes — streaming adds latency components per token, and if you have many tiny flushes we see queuing at the runtime. Non-streaming can hide per-token latency but increases tail if a request waits in a batch. For p99 you often need to tune batch size and max-wait timers.
[01:40] [00:01:40] Evelyn Park: When you say queuing, are you referring to GPU-side queueing or network queuing?
[01:45] Raj Patel: Both. There's an initial queue to build a batch on the CPU scheduler, and if your network path has extra hops (VPC NAT, on-prem firewall, sidecar proxies) each adds ms variance. On GPU side, large batches can push through but warmup and kernel launch variability influences p99.
[01:58] Maya Chen: Also important is the KV cache behavior — if the cache hits 70% for recurring prefixes you'll see big wins in average and tail, but if routing bounces requests across nodes you lose the benefit.
[02:08] Marco Diaz: Our routing is region-aware but not affinity-based, so we suspect KV cache thrash. Any suggestions?
[02:14] Raj Patel: We recommend sticky routing for short lived sessions or a lightweight routing table keyed by user/session to increase affinity. On Dedicated/Private you can also colocate inference shards that hold the KV caches for high-hit workloads.
[02:26] [00:02:26] Liam O'Connor: How about quantization — we've been looking at int8 to save cost. Does quantization affect tail?
[02:33] Raj Patel: Quantization reduces per-token compute and memory footprint, but depending on kernel implementation it can add variance. For example int8 GEMM paths sometimes use different kernel tiling which can have slightly higher jitter on cold runs. But overall int8 tends to reduce both p95 and p99 if your workload is compute bound.
[02:50] Maya Chen: Important caveat — if you're memory bound (large context, big KV cache state), quantization helps reduce memory pressure and avoids swapping which otherwise explodes tail.
[02:59] Evelyn Park: We saw occasional 500ms spikes when a node hit swap during big multi-session workloads, that might be it.
[03:05] Raj Patel: Yep. Also look at GPU memory fragmentation over time; for long-running kernels and KV cache operations fragmentation can cause allocation latency spikes. Restart cadence or memory pooling helps.
[03:18] [00:03:18] Hannah Lee: Can you walk through an example benchmark setup to isolate p99 for streaming vs batch?
[03:24] Raj Patel: Sure. Step one: replay real traffic traces — ideally same arrival patterns, payload sizes, and session continuity. Step two: run two modes: streaming (token-by-token flush) and non-streaming (aggregate full response). Collect per-token and end-to-end latencies, and log kernel-level timings if possible. Use synthetic tails by injecting small percentage of large context sessions to simulate tail behavior.
[03:43] Maya Chen: We'll provide a benchmark config. Raj, also include endpoints to collect per-stage timings — network hop, request queue, batch assemble, GPU compute, token flush.
[03:55] Raj Patel: Yep — and instrument KV cache hit/miss ratio and batch sizes over time. For p99, look at the left tail of batch assemble time; often one slow CPU process or GC can make that skew.
[04:07] [00:04:07] Marco Diaz: About networking — we have a VPC with a private subnet peered to vendor cloud; there's two NAT hops and a sidecar for egress. Are those extra hops the main source of jitter?
[04:16] Raj Patel: They can be. Each NAT or proxy adds both latency and variance. For very low-latency goals we prefer direct peering or PrivateLink-style connectivity to remove NAT. On-prem environments commonly add 2–4ms per hop but jitter is variable.
[04:29] Evelyn Park: If we do PrivateLink, do we still need to tune batching?
[04:33] Raj Patel: Yes — network variance goes down, but local queuing and GPU variability remain. Batching policy is still the main lever for throughput vs tail control.
[04:40] [00:04:40] Liam O'Connor: Can you explain dynamic batching trade-offs? We saw increased p99 after enabling bigger dynamic batches.
[04:47] Raj Patel: Dynamic batching groups small concurrent requests into larger kernels — great for throughput/cost. But if traffic isn't steady, a request might wait up to max-wait to reach batch size causing latency spikes. For p99 you lower max-wait and prefer smaller max-batch or hybrid: small steady batch for low-latency paths and separate high-throughput route.
[05:05] Maya Chen: Redwood has a two-tier policy in the platform — latency-critical requests hit a low-latency pool with small batch windows; best-effort traffic goes to high-batch pools. We can map routes by headers or model route.
[05:17] [00:05:17] Hannah Lee: Is there an easy way to measure which part of the pipeline is causing p99?
[05:21] Raj Patel: Break the tracing into segments. Add micro-timestamps: client-send, ingress-lb, edge-proxy, service-queue, batch-assemble, gpu-start, gpu-end, response-flush. Compare percentile across stages. Often p99 is dominated by a single stage — e.g., batch-assemble or proxy retries.
[05:38] Maya Chen: We'll share a span-level example in the runbook.
[05:42] [00:05:42] Marco Diaz: On private/on-prem, what's the recommended network topology? We want to avoid NAT and reduce hops.
[05:48] Raj Patel: Recommended: colocate model servers in the same subnet as the app logically, use direct peering or PrivateLink, avoid sidecar egress for token path, and keep telemetry/export out-of-band. For on-prem, run the inference nodes behind a high-speed L2 or L3 fabric and use SR-IOV or DPDK where possible for lower jitter.
[06:06] Evelyn Park: We don't have DPDK today. Could we still hit p99 targets with standard NICs?
[06:10] Raj Patel: Yes — lots of customers hit tight p99s without DPDK by focusing on affinity, reduced hops, and tuned batch windows. DPDK helps at very high QPS.
[06:19] [00:06:19] Liam O'Connor: Any gotchas with streaming flush sizes? We have a token flush every 6 tokens currently.
[06:25] Raj Patel: Flush cadence interacts with network MTU and TCP Nagle; lots of small writes can increase syscall overhead. Consider grouping small flushes or using gRPC streaming with flow control tuning. Also set appropriate socket options (TCP_NODELAY as needed) and keep-alives.
[06:41] Maya Chen: We also see customers trim early tokens to reduce variance — that is you send a light preamble and then the heavy model work. But that changes semantics so tradeoffs exist.
[06:51] [00:06:51] Hannah Lee: On quantization, you mentioned kernel differences earlier — are there model families where quantization is more jittery?
[06:58] Raj Patel: Smaller/lighter transformer variants usually have well-optimized quantized paths. Very wide models or bespoke attention may have less mature int8 kernels and thus slightly more variance, but that gap closes as we ship optimized kernels. Always validate per-model.
[07:12] [00:07:12] Marco Diaz: How about cold-start for GPU instances? We see initial requests spike.
[07:17] Raj Patel: Cold-starts are real — model load and kernel JIT can cause large spikes. Solutions: keep warm preloaded pools, use model snapshotting, or share instances across similar models. On Dedicated you can keep a minimal warm fleet.
[07:30] Evelyn Park: For our use case we need under 300ms p99 for short chats. Do you think that's achievable on Private with our traffic?
[07:37] Raj Patel: Likely yes — if you implement sticky routing, increase KV cache hit rate to >60%, reduce network hops, and run a low-latency batch pool with small max-wait. We'll propose concrete parameter ranges in the benchmark config.
[07:48] [00:07:48] Maya Chen: Quick pause — check if any blockers from security/compliance for on-prem?
[07:52] Liam O'Connor: We need KMS integration, audit logs, and role-based access. We also have a SOC2 requirement.
[07:59] Sofia Ortega: Redwood Private supports KMS/HSM integrations and audit logs; we'll attach the SOC2 artifact. We'll include RBAC examples for the private control plane.
[08:09] Raj Patel: For the bench, include encrypted payloads in traces or a sanitized replay. We'll provide scripts to replay safely.
[08:16] [00:08:16] Hannah Lee: About cost — if we do dedicated low-latency pool plus on-prem hybrid how does that impact unit economics?
[08:22] Maya Chen: Cost is higher for low-latency reserved capacity but you gain predictability. We have a cost/per-token model and also reserved capacity pricing; we'll send you a rough estimate given target p99 and QPS.
[08:33] [00:08:33] Marco Diaz: Any quick tips to reduce tail right now without infra changes?
[08:37] Raj Patel: Short list: reduce max-wait for batches, add small session affinity layer, bump KV cache TTL to avoid early eviction, and set aggressive memory pooling to avoid allocations. Also add heartbeat to detect slow nodes and route around them.
[08:53] Maya Chen: We'll include these in the recap.
[08:56] [00:08:56] Evelyn Park: One more — what instrumentation do you recommend for KV cache metrics?
[09:00] Raj Patel: Track hits/misses per prefix, per-node cache occupancy, evictions/sec, and latency per lookup. Expose these as spans so you can correlate a KV miss to a p99 event.
[09:11] [00:09:11] Liam O'Connor: Sounds good. Let's talk schedule — we can hand over traces by EOD Thursday.
[09:15] Maya Chen: Great. Raj will prepare bench config and runbook. We'll schedule a pilot run and a follow-up in ~1 week after initial runs.
[09:22] [00:09:22] Maya Chen: Any final Qs?
[09:24] Hannah Lee: Not from product. Thanks.
[09:26] Marco Diaz: No, good session.
[09:27] Raj Patel: Thanks — action items noted.
[09:29] Maya Chen: Ok we’ll send the docs and next steps. Thanks everyone.
[09:33] [END]
